title: Oko · oczy
title_en: The plural that is a different word
note: C1 Block 4, unit 4 - the block's closer, and deliberately the small one. THREE NEW STRINGS ONLY: oczy, uszy, rece. a2_plural_nom fenced these three suppletives by name; this pays that fence. THE ANCHOR IS dzieci, TAUGHT <- a2_family2 [58], verified with check_new.py rather than inherited from the inbox, which had wrongly listed dzieci as still owing a unit. SCOPE FORK, TAKEN CONSERVATIVELY AND LOGGED: the plural OBLIQUES of these three (oczu, uszu, rak, rekach, rekami/rekoma, oczami/oczyma) are OUT. They are a second system - the genitive plural of ock and ucho takes an -u found nowhere else in the course, and rak carries an e->a nasal shift that nothing has explained - so folding them in would make a small closing unit into the densest node of Block 4, against the load-splitting rule and against batch 6's own digest note that this unit is where the block should slow down. Nothing in the unit needs them: every frame here is Nominative or Accusative, and the non-virile Acc=Nom fact makes those the same form. WHAT THE RULES PREDICT IS STATED WITHOUT PRINTING A FALSE FORM: the slide names the ENDING the learner's rule points at (the neuter -a; the k/g -i) rather than writing *oka / *ucha, because those two strings are real Polish genitive singulars and marking them wrong would plant a mis-learning. That is the same discipline c1_irreg_virile used with bratom, one step more careful because these candidates are real words. THE reki OBSERVATION IS THE UNIT'S SHARPEST: the shape the k/g rule predicts for the plural of reka is reki, which the learner has OWNED since a1_gen_ki [39] as the Genitive singular - so the prediction is not merely wrong, it is already spoken for by another job. reki is used as a quiz distractor for exactly that reason and is named on the slide, per the homograph rule. THE DUAL IS TAUGHT AS HISTORY, NOT AS A RULE: AGENTS pitches the register for a linguistically-inclined adult, and the fact that these are the surviving dual forms of the three things that come in pairs is the best possible hook for three arbitrary words - but the slide says plainly that it cannot be used to build anything new. nogi is NOT used anywhere: it is TAUGHT <- a1_gen_ki [39] as a Genitive singular, and using it as the regular plural counterexample would be the homograph trap in the very unit that warns about it; the counterexample stays in English. myje rece was refused too - myc is owned only as the reflexive myje sie (a2_sie), so a transitive object would be a new fact.

intro.title: One plural you already have that is not built from its singular
intro.body:
You have been saying dzieci since A2 without looking at it closely. It is worth a look. dziecko is neuter, and the neuter plural rule you own turns -o into -a. dzieci is not that. It is not reached from dziecko by any ending in the course.

Three more nouns do the same thing, and they are three of the most useful words in the body vocabulary you learned at A1: oko, ucho, ręka.

For these four, the plural is a word of its own. You learn it once, and after that everything about it is ordinary.
intro.body_pl: dziecko → dzieci · oko → oczy · ucho → uszy · ręka → ręce

intro.title: What your own rules point at — and why they miss
intro.body:
oko and ucho are neuter, so the rule you have points at the neuter ending. ręka is feminine and its stem ends in -k, so the k/g rule points at the ending -i. Neither prediction is the plural.

ręka is the sharper of the two, because the shape the rule predicts is a form you already own: ręki is the Genitive singular, learned back at A1. So the prediction is not just wrong here — that shape is already doing another job in the language.

This is the reason the three have to be learned rather than worked out.
intro.body_pl: oko · ucho · ręka — rodzaj nijaki i żeński

headers: The ending your rule points at
The plural that is actually there
rows: — and -i is taken: ręki is the Genitive singular

intro.title: Why exactly these three, and not the leg or the finger
intro.body:
There is a reason, and it is a good place to hang three arbitrary words.

Old Polish had a third number, between the singular and the plural: a dual, used for things that come in twos. It disappeared from the language centuries ago — except in a few words, where the old dual form simply stayed on and became the modern plural. Eyes, ears and hands come in pairs. That is why these three, and not the leg, the finger or the tooth.

It is history, not a rule. You cannot use it to build a new word: nothing else in modern Polish counts in twos any more. It only explains the ones that are already there.

intro.title: Nothing else in the sentence notices
intro.title_pl: te oczy · moje ręce · duże uszy
intro.body:
Once you have the plural itself, no new agreement comes with it. All three are non-virile plurals — things, not groups of men — so everything in front of them takes the plural forms you have had since A2: te, moje, duże, małe.

And because they are non-virile, the Accusative is the same as the Nominative. Mam małe ręce uses exactly the form that stands as the subject in Moje ręce są małe. One form, both jobs.

rows: Accusative = Nominative in the non-virile plural

intro.title: What to carry away
intro.body:
Three plurals to learn as words, plus the one you have had since A2 keeping them company.

That closes the plural. Between the softening families, the -owie family, the four person-nouns with their own stem and these three, every plural this course owes you is now on the table.
intro.body_pl: oko → oczy · ucho → uszy · ręka → ręce

quiz.prompt: Te ___ są duże. (these eyes are big)
quiz.explain: The plural of oko is a word of its own — it is not built from oko by an ending.
bolą is the plural, so more than one ear: uszy. One ear would be boli mnie ucho.
ręki is the shape the k/g rule points at — but it is the Genitive singular you learned at A1, not the plural.

quiz.prompt: To jest moje ___. (this is my eye — one)
quiz.explain: One of them, so the plain dictionary form: oko, neuter, hence moje.

quiz.prompt: Dziecko ma małe ___. (the child has small ears)
quiz.explain: Accusative after ma — and in the non-virile plural that is the same form as the Nominative.

quiz.prompt: Moja ___ jest mała. (my hand is small — one)
quiz.explain: One hand: the dictionary form. ręki is the Genitive singular and is not a subject.

quiz.prompt: Te ___ mają duże oczy. (these children have big eyes)
quiz.explain: The subject of the sentence, so the Nominative plural — the one you have had since A2.

quiz.prompt: Mama ma zmęczone ___. (mum has tired eyes)
quiz.explain: zmęczone is the non-virile plural adjective, so it is pointing at a non-virile plural noun.

quiz.prompt: Ten człowiek ma duże ___. (this man has big ears)
quiz.explain: The noun is a thing, not a group of men, so nothing virile happens here — only the plural itself is unusual.

quiz.prompt: Moje ___ są małe. (my hands are small)
quiz.explain: The subject, and the same form you would use as an object: Mam małe ręce.

quiz.prompt: ___ oczy są duże. (these eyes are big)
quiz.explain: oczy is a non-virile plural, so te — exactly as with okna or gazety.
boli is singular, so one ear. The verb tells you the number before the noun does.

type_items.explain: A word of its own — the surviving old form for a pair.
Same story as oczy: a pair word that stayed.
Not ręki — that shape is the Genitive singular and was taken long ago.
One of a pair, so the ordinary singular.
The singular is completely regular; only the plural is odd.
The oldest member of this small family, owned since A2.
oczy is a non-virile plural, so the adjective takes -e.
